fetched_contents.text: Crystallization kinetics of citric acid anhydrate Highlights * • The solubility and metastable zone width of citric acid anhydrate were measured. * • Nucleation kinetic parameters were estimated by Nyvlt's method. * • A desupersaturation curve method was employed to estimate crystal growth. * • A dimension variation of a single crystal was also used to estimate growth rate. * • Both methods were compared. Abstract The solubility curve, metastable zone width (MSZW) and Crystallization kinetics (nucleation and growth) were measured and estimated during batch crystallization of citric acid anhydrate (CAA). The solubility of citric acid in pure water was measured over the temperature range from 15 to 60 °C using a refractometer. The experimental data were correlated by the modified Apelblat equation. The MSZW was determined under four cooling rates for different citric acid concentrations by means of an ultrasonic technique. The primary nucleation kinetics of CAA was calculated based on these data and the polythermal method of Nyvlt. It was found that the MSZW obtained is in good agreement with literature. Crystal growth rates were calculated by two methods. The first one used seeded isothermal growth experiments (desupersaturation curve) and the derivatives method of Garside. The second method used the measurement of the dimension change of a single crystal in a microscopic cell at different supersaturation levels. Introduction Crystallization is an important step in the purification of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) during the development process. Over 80% of drug products are produced by at least one crystallization step [1]. Two major steps govern the crystallization process, nucleation and crystal growth. The driving force for both steps is supersaturation defined as the difference between the actual concentration of the solute and the saturation concentration (solubility).The region between the solubility curve and the onset of nucleation phenomenon, called metastable zone width (MSZW), defines an operating boundary during crystallization process [2]. The MSZW depends on different process variables such as cooling rate, solvent composition, stirring rate and impurities [3]. Accurate modeling of crystallization kinetics, in particular the solubility curve, MSZW and the nucleation is an essential prerequisite to the design and control of a given crystallization process [4]. Citric acid plays an exceptional role, among the fruit acids used in beverage, food, pharmaceutical, textile, metal, chemical and other industries. Worldwide, citric acid is commercially produced in million tones with a steady annual increase in consumption and production [5]. At room temperature, citric acid exists in a white crystalline powder either in anhydrous form (CAA) or monohydrate form (CAM). Anhydrous citric acid differs from the monohydrate in terms of solubility, bioavailability and crystal packing. The transition from the anhydrous to the monohydrate polymorphic form occurs in the range 34 −36 °C [6], [7], [8]. Citric acid monohydrate crystallization has been extensively studied in several research papers, but only few have been interested to the anhydrous form. Laguerie et al. [9] reported the solubility and other physical properties of CAM aqueous solutions. Nyvlt and Vaclavu [2] investigated the crystal growth of a CAM monocrystal at 32 and 12 °C. The growth order ranged from 1.9 to 2 depending on the operating conditions. Laguerie and Angelino [10] and Laguerie et al. [11] investigated the growth kinetics of large CAM crystals (>1.4 mm) in a fluidized bed at 25 °C and found a growth order equal to 1.04. Sikdar and Randolph [12] studied very small crystals (70 µm) in mixed crystallizer and obtained a growth rate order equal to 0.65. Bravi et al. [13] performed solubility and primary nucleation kinetics of pure and selectively impure CAM solutions. In order to provide a critical comparison of the available data, Bravi et al. [14] have studied, in another paper, the crystal growth of CAM in a fluidized bed crystallizer or in the cell of a laser light diffraction granulometer, using seed sizes intermediate between those adopted by previous researchers [11], [12]. The crystallization and dissolution behavior of the system citric acid-water has been previously studied using temperature-programmed and isothermal batch experiments [15]. In this last work, the mother-phase supersaturation and turbidity have been monitored on-line via simultaneous measurements using attenuated total reflection (ATR) Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and optical turbidometric detection, respectively. The study reveals through the phase diagram a very wide MSZW width and that anhydrate phase crystallized by temperature-programmed runs while the monohydrate was formed by isothermal batch crystallization experiments. Batch seeded isothermal crystallization of monohydrate citric acid in water was also investigated as the first stage of a wider study devoted to the modeling of the anhydrous to monohydrate phase transition of citric acid at 15 °C (i.e., below the transition point of the system.) [16]. More recently, Helmdach et al. [6] evaluated the applicability of the ultrasonic technique in determining the solubility and the MSZW of 12 organic and inorganic compounds including some pharmaceutical ones. Among these substances citric acid has shown an excellent applicability. In another paper, Helmdach and coworkers [17] have demonstrated that the ultrasound technique, a cheap and robust method, allows the detection of the metastable zone width and an in- line control of supersaturation as well as the indirect control of phase transition in the system citric acid-water. fetched_contents.text: Citric Acid Production Equipment: A 7-Step Industrial Guide Introduction Citric acid is a cornerstone commodity chemical, indispensable in the food and beverage, pharmaceutical, and cleaning industries for its roles as a preservative, acidulant, and chelating agent. The transition from laboratory-scale synthesis to large-scale industrial manufacturing hinges on a sophisticated array of Citric Acid Production Equipment. This machinery is not a single unit but a complex, integrated system designed to manage a delicate biochemical process with precision and efficiency. Understanding the components and their functions is crucial for any enterprise looking to enter or optimize its position in this competitive market. The entire workflow, from raw material handling to the final crystallized product, relies on specialized hardware designed for sterility, control, and high yield, making the selection of this equipment a primary determinant of a facility's success. The Foundation of Production: Raw Material and Media Preparation The journey to producing citric acid begins long before any fermentation occurs. It starts with the meticulous preparation of the substrate, the nutrient-rich medium that will feed the microorganisms responsible for production. The most common substrates are carbohydrate-rich materials like corn starch, cassava, or molasses from sugar cane or beets. The initial stage of equipment includes large storage silos and tanks, conveyance systems, and hydrolysis reactors. In these reactors, starches are broken down into simpler sugars, like glucose, through enzymatic or acid hydrolysis. The precision of this stage is paramount, as the purity of the medium directly influences the efficiency of the Citric Acid Fermentation Process. Once sterilized, the liquid medium is transferred to a media hold tank where essential nutrients and minerals are added. This includes a source of nitrogen (like ammonia or ammonium salts), phosphorus (like phosphates), and various trace elements (such as magnesium, zinc, and iron) that are vital for the health and productivity of the fungal culture. The pH of the medium is also carefully adjusted to a specific range, typically between 2.0 and 5.0, depending on the specific strain of microorganism used. In addition, chromatography services are mentioned as supporting methods for trace metal analysis and broader chemical composition analysis, with services such as HPLC-DAD, GC-MS, and GC-IR being referenced in the evidence set [N4-R3]. The evidence also mentions HPLC-ICP-MS as a method for quantifying dissolved AsIII and AsV in extracts, suggesting that coupling chromatography with mass spectrometry can separate and detect trace impurities in complex matrices [N4-R5]. Overall, the main analytical methods in the evidence are ICP-MS, chromatography, and compositional analysis, with a clear emphasis on trace metal quantification and multi-element detection [N4-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5].

How routine monitoring and process control data support purity maintenance
The evidence shows that analytical data and process control data are closely tied to maintaining purity. The industrial crystallization source notes that the foundation of production begins with raw material and media preparation, and that the purity of the medium directly influences the efficiency of fermentation [N5-F4]. This implies that monitoring raw-material quality and media composition is part of the purity control strategy. The same source emphasizes that the fermentation stage depends on precise control of temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, and other parameters [N5-F4], which are routine process-monitoring variables that help maintain a consistent environment. While the evidence does not explicitly mention process control data being used in real time for purity correction, it does establish that process control is a prerequisite for high-purity production: the fermentation equipment must be reliable, precise, and designed for aseptic operation [N5-F4]. This means that process-monitoring data supports purity by maintaining optimal conditions that reduce contamination risk and ensure reproducibility.

Limitations and trade-offs of different analytical approaches
The evidence indicates several trade-offs among analytical approaches. ICP-MS is praised for its sensitivity and multi-element capability, but it is also described as “challenging matrices”-specific, suggesting that matrix effects can complicate interpretation [N4-F3]. Chromatography-based methods, such as HPLC-DAD and GC-MS, are useful but may require complex sample preparation and may not capture all impurity classes equally [N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also suggests that different methods are suited to different purposes: HPLC-ICP-MS is useful for trace metal speciation, whereas compositional analysis services are broad but less specific about impurity classes [N4-R5][N4-F3]. Another trade-off is speed versus specificity: online sequential fractionation analysis is noted as a technique that allows detailed arsenic speciation, but the excerpt does not describe it as routine or low-cost [N4-R5]. Overall, the methods are complementary rather than interchangeable, and the evidence supports a balanced approach that uses ICP-MS for trace metal screening and chromatography for organic and speciated impurities [N4-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Bottom line
The analytical branch of the evidence supports a layered strategy: ICP-MS for trace metal quantification, chromatography for organic impurities, and compositional analysis for broader chemical verification [N4-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5]. Routine monitoring of process variables such as temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen helps maintain consistent conditions that support purity [N5-F4].
